title: Pricing Strategy for B2B SaaS
summary: Patrick Campbell, founder of ProfitWell and pricing expert, breaks down pricing strategy for B2B SaaS companies. Topics include value metrics, pricing page design, and when to change your pricing.
transcript:
Lenny: Welcome back to the podcast. Today's episode is all about pricing, one of the most important and least understood aspects of building a SaaS business. I'm joined by Patrick Campbell, founder of ProfitWell. Patrick, welcome.

Patrick: Thanks for having me, Lenny. Excited to talk pricing.

Lenny: Let's start with the basics. Why do so many companies struggle with pricing?

Patrick: Most companies treat pricing as an afterthought. They spend months building features but only a few hours thinking about pricing. This is backwards. Pricing is your most powerful growth lever - it impacts every part of your business from customer acquisition to retention to expansion.

Lenny: What should companies be thinking about when they set their pricing?

Patrick: The most important concept is your value metric - what you charge for. This should align with where you deliver value. If your product saves customers time, charge based on time saved or users. If you process transactions, charge based on transaction volume. The value metric should scale with customer value.

Lenny: Can you give examples of good and bad value metrics?

Patrick: Sure. Slack charges per active user - that's great because more users means more value. Mailchimp charges per contact - also good because more contacts means more value. A bad example would be charging per login or per API call if those don't correlate with customer value.

Lenny: What about the actual price points? How do you determine what to charge?

Patrick: This is where willingness-to-pay research comes in. You need to talk to customers and prospects about what they'd pay. Not hypothetically, but based on the value you're delivering. I recommend talking to at least 20-30 customers to get a sense of the range.

Lenny: Should you show pricing on your website?

Patrick: For most B2B SaaS, yes. Transparency builds trust. But there's a caveat - if your pricing is complex or highly customized, you might need a 'contact sales' option for larger customers. The key is to show enough to qualify leads while not scaring away good prospects.

Lenny: Let's talk about pricing tiers. How many should you have?

Patrick: Three is usually optimal - a basic tier, a professional tier, and an enterprise tier. The middle tier is typically your sweet spot. The basic tier exists to capture smaller customers and show price-conscious buyers you're accessible. The enterprise tier captures large customers and makes the middle tier look reasonable.

Lenny: What's a common mistake with tiering?

Patrick: Making the tiers too similar. Each tier needs clear differentiation. The value you deliver should increase significantly at each level. If customers can't easily understand the difference, they'll default to the cheapest option.

Lenny: When should a company change their pricing?

Patrick: You should review pricing annually, but only change it when you have strong evidence. Signs you need to change: you're consistently getting pushback on price, you're leaving money on the table with easy wins, or your value delivery has changed significantly.

Lenny: How do you handle changing pricing for existing customers?

Patrick: Grandfather them if possible. It builds goodwill and avoids churn. If you must raise prices for everyone, give plenty of notice - at least 3-6 months. And make sure you're delivering more value to justify the increase.

Lenny: What about discounting? When is it appropriate?

Patrick: Sparingly. Every discount trains customers to expect more discounts. If you do discount, tie it to something - annual vs monthly payment, case study participation, early adopter status. Never discount just because someone asks.

Lenny: Let's talk about expansion revenue. How does pricing relate to net revenue retention?

Patrick: Your pricing model should make expansion natural. If you're charging per user, growth in team size drives expansion. If you're charging per usage, increased activity drives revenue. The best SaaS companies have net revenue retention above 120% because their pricing expands as customers grow.

Lenny: What's your take on freemium?

Patrick: Freemium can work, but it's harder than people think. You need a low cost to serve free users, a clear upgrade path, and enough volume to make the conversion math work. For most B2B SaaS, a free trial is better than freemium.

Lenny: Why is that?

Patrick: Free trials create urgency. Users know they have limited time to evaluate, so they engage more deeply. Freemium users often stay free forever without engaging much. Unless you're building a PLG motion with viral components, trials are more effective.

Lenny: How long should a free trial be?

Patrick: 14 days is standard, but the right length depends on your time-to-value. If users can realize value in a day, a 7-day trial works. If it takes weeks to see value, you might need 30 days. The key is to align trial length with how long it takes to get to an aha moment.

Lenny: What about packaging - bundling features together?

Patrick: Packaging is as important as pricing. Bundle features by persona or use case, not by technical architecture. Your pricing tiers should map to different customer segments with different needs and budgets.

Lenny: Final question. What's the one pricing mistake that costs companies the most money?

Patrick: Underpricing. Most founders underprice out of fear. They think lower prices mean more customers, but that's often wrong. Higher prices attract better customers, improve your LTV:CAC ratio, and give you resources to deliver more value. Charge what you're worth.

Lenny: Brilliant advice. Patrick, this has been incredibly insightful. Thank you for breaking down pricing so clearly.

Patrick: My pleasure, Lenny. Pricing is fascinating once you dive in.
